claims.text: An ML potential trained on high-fidelity ab initio data from both solid and liquid phases near melting can reproduce accurate fusion free energies and associated thermodynamic observables.
The ML-accelerated workflow can operate at a fraction of the computational cost of explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD.
The initial scope is elemental and binary systems near their melting transitions.
The ML potential will be trained on representative solid- and liquid-phase ab initio energies, forces, and vibrational properties.
Thermodynamic integration or another enhanced-sampling method will be used with the ML potential to compute phase free energies.
Using the ML surrogate can preserve key entropy contributions, including anharmonic and electron–vibration effects.
The workflow should cover temperatures below and above the melting point.
High-quality AIMD and TOR-TILD free-energy benchmark data exist for suitable well-characterized elemental and binary systems.
The ML potential mediates between microscopic atomic configurations and macroscopic phase free energies.
Training on both solid and liquid data enables the ML potential to capture structural complexity and relevant entropy contributions.
Ab initio training data can encode anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling effects in both phases.
The trained ML model can interpolate the complex energy landscape near the phase transition.
Combining the ML model with enhanced sampling permits phase-free-energy evaluation with accuracy comparable to full AIMD at substantially lower cost.
The workflow will achieve a speed-up of approximately one to two orders of magnitude over explicit AIMD workflows.
Free energies and melting-point predictions will agree with TOR-TILD and AIMD benchmarks to chemical accuracy, described as deviations of a few meV per atom.
The hypothesis is expected to hold for elemental and binary systems near their phase-transition temperatures.
Extension to multicomponent high-entropy alloys may be limited by increased configurational complexity and sparse training data.

The hypothesis is falsified if phase free energies or melting temperature differ from matched AIMD or TOR-TILD benchmarks by more than approximately 5% or fall outside the stated chemical-accuracy target.
